title: AI Tools at Yale for Researchers
text:
Five terms worth knowing

Key terms






Term
Meaning




Model
The AI itself: GPT, Claude, Gemini. New versions every few months


Agent
A model that can take steps: search, run code, use tools. In Clarity, the menu of models


Hallucination
A confident answer that’s false, such as a made-up citation


Web search
Answers based on current web pages, with links, rather than training data alone


Deep research
Many searches, read and summarized into a long, sourced report

title: Yale’s AI Tools
text:
Clarity
Yale’s own AI chat platform, free for current students, staff and faculty. Clarity at ai.yale.edu

Sign in: go to clarity-ai.yale.edu and log in with your Yale account.
Models: choose an “agent” for a model from OpenAI, Anthropic (Claude) or Google (Gemini). The agents page lists the current ones.
Beta agents (through December 2026): newer models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google to try, labeled Beta in the agent menu. They support low-, moderate- and high-risk data, and the Health beta agents also support ePHI. They’re less tested, may change or be removed, and aren’t available in custom agents. For critical or time-sensitive work, use a featured agent. (announcement)
What’s new (October 2026 Agent Portal): image generation, voice conversations, chat search and tags, mobile use, and connections to other tools. (release notes)
Web search: built into every featured agent, including the Health agents, since November 18, 2026. The separate Radiate pilot agent is being removed. (announcement) Yale’s Clarity page approves web search for up to high-risk data, but another line on the same page still says low risk only. Until Yale confirms, keep ePHI and other high-risk details out of questions that send Clarity to the web.
Files: upload up to 10 files at a time.
Custom agents: build your own assistant with standing instructions and reference files, after your use case is approved. (custom agents) Owners can turn on web search under Manage Agents > Tools > Gemini Web Grounding.
Data: approved for low, moderate and most high-risk data. Not for NIST 800-171 data. Data under a data use agreement needs checking first. Your data isn’t used to train the models. (security)
ePHI: only in the Health agents, which you request through ServiceNow. (Health agents)







TipIf you used Clarity before October 2026



The interface and the model list changed. Old models such as GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 were replaced, and Clarity can now search the web. Some older Yale pages still describe the previous version.

title: Rules of the Road
text:
The short version

Match the tool to the data. Use only Yale-approved tools for anything beyond public information. See Start with your data.
You’re responsible for everything you submit. AI can’t be an author, and “the AI wrote it” isn’t a defense.
Check every citation. Presenting an AI-invented reference as real can be treated as fabrication.
Disclose AI use where the funder or journal asks for it.
Never use AI on someone else’s confidential work you’re reviewing: grant applications or manuscripts.

title: Rules of the Road
text:
NIH

NIH rules on AI use


Rule
What it means for you
Source




Applications “substantially developed by AI” won’t be considered
Write the science yourself. AI can help you edit, check or brainstorm, but NIH uses detection tools, and misuse found after an award can lead to referral to the Office of Research Integrity and to the award being suspended or terminated.
NOT-OD-25-132


Six applications per PI per calendar year
New, renewal, resubmission and revision applications count; T awards and R13s don’t.
NOT-OD-25-132


AI-invented references
Presenting them as real “could constitute data fabrication.” Reckless AI use can be research misconduct. Describe how you used AI.
NIH reminder, May 2026


No AI in peer review
Reviewers may not put any part of an application into an AI tool or use AI to write a critique.
NOT-OD-23-149


Controlled-access data
Putting NIH controlled-access data (such as dbGaP) into public AI tools violates your Data Use Certification.
NOT-OD-25-081

title: Rules of the Road
text:
Journals
Most journals follow the ICMJE recommendations on AI:

AI tools can’t be listed as authors, or cited as a primary source.
Disclose AI use, usually in the cover letter and in the Methods or Acknowledgments.
Authors are responsible for checking AI-assisted text and images for accuracy and plagiarism.

Publishers add their own rules, and they change often. Recent examples:

Elsevier (updated August 2026): an AI declaration at submission; AI may not create or alter research images such as blots, microscopy or patient images. Basic grammar and spelling tools don’t need declaring. (Elsevier)
JAMA Network: name the tool, version and maker; don’t use AI to generate reference lists; reviewers must not put manuscripts into AI tools. (JAMA instructions for authors)







TipBefore you submit



Read the specific journal’s “use of AI” section in its author instructions. Keep a short note of which tool you used, its version, the date and what you used it for, so the disclosure is easy to write.

title: Rules of the Road
text:
Yale

Data classification: don’t put moderate- or high-risk data into tools not approved for that level. (Policy 1604; AI guidelines)
Patient data (PHI): use it in AI tools only when it’s essential and covered by your IRB protocol. Use the minimum needed; prefer de-identified or synthetic data. Removing names isn’t de-identification. A vendor saying “HIPAA-compliant” isn’t approval. (Using AI safely in health care)
Library-licensed content: generally, don’t upload articles, e-books or database content from Yale Library subscriptions into AI tools. (Library AI guidance)
Data use agreements: a DUA may forbid AI processing even in an approved tool. Check before you upload.
Provost guidelines: assume what you enter in an unapproved tool could become public, and you’re responsible for what you produce. (Provost guidelines)







NoteHuman subjects research



If you plan to use AI to process participant data, for example to code interviews or analyze survey responses, check with the Human Research Protection Program on whether your protocol and consent forms need to say so.

title: Prompting and Checking
section: Five parts of a good prompt
text:
Five parts of a good prompt
You don’t need all five every time, but the more of them a prompt has, the less you’ll need to correct afterward.

Five parts of an effective prompt







Part
What to include
Example




Task
A clear verb and a specific goal. Break big jobs into steps.
“Draft three versions of a recruitment flyer headline…”


Context
Background, constraints, audience, what success looks like
“…for a study of young adults who use nicotine pouches. IRB-approved wording must stay unchanged…”


Examples
A sample of what good (and bad) output looks like
“Here’s a headline we liked from a previous study: …”


Format
Structure, length, how to mark changes
“…under 12 words each, as a numbered list”


Tone
Voice and reading level
“…friendly, not alarming, 8th-grade reading level.”




Habits that help

Let it ask you questions first. End with: “Before you start, ask me any questions you need answered.”
Iterate. Treat the first answer as a draft. Say what to change and why.
Give it the source. Paste or upload the document (if the data level allows) instead of asking from memory. Answers grounded in a source are more accurate.
Ask for its uncertainty. “Which parts of this answer are you least sure about?”
Start a new chat for a new topic. Long chats drift, and earlier material can crowd out what matters now.
Save prompts that work. In Clarity you can turn a prompt you reuse into a custom agent.

title: Prompting and Checking
text:
Check before you use it
AI output is a draft from a fast, confident assistant who is sometimes wrong. Before you use it:

Citations: does each reference exist, and does it say what’s claimed? Look it up in PubMed or the publisher’s site, not in the AI tool.
Numbers: recalculate any statistic, dose or count that matters.
Code: run it on test data where you know the right answer. Read what it does before running it on real data.
Currency: is this information current? Models have a training cutoff unless they searched the web.
Omissions: what would an expert in your field add or push back on?
Bias and framing: does the output stereotype a population or assume one point of view?
Disclosure: do the funder or journal need to know you used AI for this?

In beta: AI search of Yale Library’s catalog
Yale Library’s AI Connector lets AI assistants such as Claude and ChatGPT search almost 15 million records in the library catalog and nearly 185,000 in its digital collections. Which assistant: Yale doesn’t provide ChatGPT, so a personal ChatGPT account is for public information only. For OpenAI’s models under your Yale account, Clarity is the alternative, but the connector doesn’t list Clarity yet; the library has named it only as a possible future option (pilot announcement).

title: Literature Tools
text:
Consensus
Consensus searches more than 250 million peer-reviewed papers (from Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and its own web crawl) and writes an answer with citations. Yale Library is running a year-long trial. (Library announcement, Yale’s Consensus page)

Getting access

Go to consensus.app and sign up with your Yale email (yale.edu, ynhh.org or ynhh.com) or Yale Google login.
The Yale trial runs through December 31, 2026. Ask the library (marx.reference@yale.edu) what happens after that.
Approved for low-risk data only. Ask questions about published research. Don’t paste unpublished results, draft manuscripts or participant data.



What it does

Search modes: Quick, Pro and Deep, which read roughly 10, 20 and 50 papers.
Consensus Meter: for yes/no questions (“Does X reduce Y?”), a bar showing how many papers lean Yes, Possibly, Mixed or No.
Study snapshots: population, sample size, methods and outcomes pulled from a paper.
Filters: study type (RCT, meta-analysis, systematic review), journal quartile, sample size, year.
Full text or abstract? A checkmark on a citation means Consensus read the full text. No checkmark means it worked from the abstract only.
Access to paywalled papers: links open through Yale’s subscriptions.



Know the limits

The Meter counts papers; it doesn’t weigh them. One large RCT and one small cross-sectional survey count the same. Published literature also over-represents positive results.
Paywalled papers are often summarized from the abstract alone.
Labels can be wrong. The study-type label is assigned by AI. Journal rank is not study quality.
Answers aren’t reproducible. The same question can give different answers in Pro and Deep mode, or on a different day.
Paid plans add more Pro and Deep searches. The free tier has monthly limits. Check current limits in the app.

These limits are discussed in Aaron Tay’s review of Consensus (2025) and in CWML’s comparison of Consensus, OpenEvidence and UpToDate (2026).






TipA good Consensus workflow




Ask a specific question: population, exposure or intervention, outcome.
Check the Meter, then filter to systematic reviews, meta-analyses or RCTs and see if the picture changes.
Open the top 3–5 papers. Check that each one says what the summary claims.
Note which answers came from abstracts only.
Use what you learn to build a proper PubMed search.

title: Literature Tools
text:
NotebookLM
NotebookLM answers questions only from the sources you put in a notebook, and every answer links back to the passage it came from. It’s free with your Yale Google account and approved for moderate-risk data. (Yale’s Gemini and NotebookLM page)
Good uses:

Compare the methods, samples and measures across 5–20 papers you’ve already chosen
Find where in a long report or guidance document something is discussed
Make a study guide or an audio overview of your lab’s papers for a new trainee







WarningWhat you may upload




Open-access papers (PubMed Central, preprints), your own manuscripts and your lab’s documents: yes, up to moderate risk.
PDFs you downloaded through Yale Library subscriptions: generally no. Publisher licenses usually forbid uploading their content to AI tools. See the library’s AI guidance for library resources.
Identifiable participant data: no. NotebookLM is approved for moderate risk only.

title: Resources
text:
Key terms

Model

The AI system that generates responses, such as GPT, Claude or Gemini. Each company releases new versions every few months.

Agent

In Clarity, a “featured agent” is a model with Yale’s settings, such as GPT or Claude Sonnet. More generally, an AI agent is a model that can take steps on its own: search, run code, use tools, and check its work.

Prompt

The instructions, question and material you give the AI.

Context window

How much text the model can work with at once: your prompt, uploaded files and the conversation so far.

Hallucination

A confident answer that’s false, such as a made-up citation, statistic or quote.

Web search (grounding)

The model searches the web and bases its answer on what it finds, with links. Without it, answers come only from training data, which has a cutoff date.

Deep research

A mode that runs many searches, reads the results and writes a long report with sources. It takes minutes, not seconds.

Token

The unit models read and charge by. Roughly ¾ of an English word.

How this site stays current
Yale’s AI tools and rules change every few months. Every day, an automated check reads ai.yale.edu and the other pages this site links to. When a source changes, an AI agent drafts an update to the site, and a human reviews and approves every change before it’s published. The “Last checked” date on each page shows when its facts were last confirmed.
If you spot something out of date, email us at justin.demayo@yale.edu.
